analysis.one_liner: Opens the Arctic refuge coast to oil drilling and cuts coal-mine cleanup fees while funding miner retiree health.
analysis.headline: The bill died without a single cosponsor, a hearing, or a vote: it sat in two House committees from June 2004 until the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill had two halves. The first opened roughly 1.5 million acres of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge coastal plain to oil and gas leasing, repealed the 1980 law's ban on production there, sped up the environmental review, and limited court challenges. The second rewrote the coal mine cleanup law: it cut the fee coal operators pay to clean up abandoned mines by 20 percent, stripped money away from rural land reclamation, and created a fund—paid for with the new Arctic oil revenues—that would cover coal companies' obligations to retired miners' health plans and refund certain companies' premiums. The bill was introduced by one House Republican, attracted no cosponsors, and was never acted on in committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies would gain access to lease one of the largest untouched onshore prospects in the country, with a guaranteed first lease sale of at least 200,000 acres within 22 months. Coal operators would pay a lower cleanup fee and would be relieved of some legacy retiree-health premiums and successor liabilities. Retired coal miners would gain guaranteed funding for their health benefits, paid out of Arctic oil revenue rather than by the companies. Alaska and local North Slope communities would get a share of leasing revenue and impact aid.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil companies, coal operators, retired miners

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the 1980 statutory prohibition on oil and gas production in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and establishes a competitive leasing program for the 1,549,000-acre coastal plain, with a first lease sale of at least 200,000 acres required within 22 months of enactment.

Requires a royalty of at least 12.5 percent, sends 50 percent of leasing revenue to the State of Alaska, caps total surface development footprint at 2,000 acres, bans export of the oil produced, and requires seasonal protections for caribou calving areas and subsistence hunting.

Cuts the abandoned mine reclamation fee paid by coal operators from 35 cents to 28 cents per ton for underground mines and from 10 cents to 8 cents for surface mines, and repeals uses of the cleanup fund for rural land reclamation and for Interior Department research contracts.

Creates a 'Coal Mining Fairness Fund' financed by the Arctic oil bonuses, rents, and royalties, which would pay the United Mine Workers Combined Benefit Fund's obligations, waive premiums owed by certain previously assigned operators, and refund $36 million in pre-2001 premiums plus 7.5 percent interest.

Limits who counts as a 'successor in interest' liable for retiree-health premiums and lets publicly traded parent companies prepay their subsidiaries' premium liability to end joint and several liability for related companies.

Requires project labor agreements for lease construction and 'best efforts' hiring of Alaska Natives, and sets up an impact-aid fund of up to $11 million for the North Slope Borough and other affected Alaska communities.

analysis.who_pays: The public would bear the environmental risk of industrial development inside a national wildlife refuge under a bill that deems leasing 'compatible' with refuge purposes, narrows the required environmental analysis to a single leasing alternative, and channels all challenges into the D.C. Circuit court with a presumption that the government's analysis is correct. Mining-region communities would have less money for cleaning up abandoned mines and acid drainage, since the operator fee would drop 20 percent and rural land reclamation grants would end. The Treasury would effectively redirect a public resource—Arctic oil revenue—to cover coal companies' retiree-health obligations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Public lands, mining communities, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The bill deems the leasing program compatible with the purposes of the Arctic refuge with 'no further findings,' and requires the Interior Secretary to analyze only one leasing alternative and a preferred action rather than nonleasing options, with only 20 days for public comments.

Court challenges would be confined to the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals within 90 days, and the Secretary's environmental analysis would be presumed correct unless disproven by clear and convincing evidence.

Cutting the reclamation fee by 20 percent reduces the stream of money available to reclaim abandoned mines and treat acid mine drainage, which is a leading source of water pollution in Appalachian and other coalfield communities; the same bill also ends federal rural land reclamation grants.

The bill would shift the cost of retired miners' health benefits onto a new federal fund financed by Arctic oil revenue, relieving specific coal companies of premiums and liabilities they would otherwise owe under the Internal Revenue Code.

Supporters of the bill would argue that the coastal plain is a small slice of the refuge with a strong environmental-protection framework and that the revenue helps fund miner benefits—but the same title strips review protections that would let the public test whether those protections are actually enforced.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The genuine benefits—guaranteed funding for retired coal miners' health care, royalties and revenue shares for Alaska, and a 2,000-acre development footprint—are real but conditional on what a later administration chooses to enforce. The bill's structural choices point the other way: it forecloses the environmental alternative analysis, funnels all litigation to one court with a presumption of government correctness, cuts the cleanup fee that pays for abandoned mine reclamation, and uses public oil revenue to retire private coal companies' legacy health liabilities. The coal provisions in particular are narrow, company-specific relief written as a national reclamation 'reform.'

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced by one House member with no cosponsors, referred to two committees, and neither committee ever took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Richard Pombo of California introduced the bill on June 14, 2004, and it was referred that day to the House Committee on Resources and to the Committee on Ways and Means.
The bill never advanced beyond those referrals: the full action history shows no hearings, markups, or floor action, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2005.
The bill drew zero cosponsors in the House.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one moved to advance or stop the bill; the outcome preserved the status quo, meaning the Arctic refuge stayed closed to drilling and the abandoned mine cleanup fee stayed at its existing rate. Coalfield communities that rely on the cleanup fund and opponents of Arctic drilling were better off than they would have been had it passed, while the oil and coal industries kept the access and relief they would have gained only on paper.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Arctic refuge stayed closed; coal cleanup fund intact

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had zero cosponsors, so no partisan split can be measured; it was a single-sponsor Republican bill that never left committee.

industries.note: The bill would give the industry access to lease roughly 1.5 million acres of the Arctic refuge coastal plain, with a mandatory first lease sale, a deemed 'compatible' finding, streamlined environmental analysis, and sharply limited court review. The industry's gain comes from a protected public resource at the public's environmental risk, though the bill does impose a 12.5 percent royalty, an export ban, and surface-footprint limits.

The bill cuts the abandoned-mine reclamation fee operators pay by 20 percent, waives premiums certain operators owe for retired miners' health care, and narrows successor liability for companies that bought coal assets at arm's length. The savings come at the expense of cleanup funding for mining communities and the retiree benefit funds' dedicated revenue stream.

industries.industry: United Mine Workers retiree health funds
industries.note: The Combined Benefit Fund and the 1992 and 1993 benefit plans would receive guaranteed payments—ultimately from Arctic oil revenue—covering retired miners' health benefits. This is the bill's clearest benefit to working people, though it is financed by redirecting public resource revenue rather than by industry contributions.

industries.industry: Abandoned mine land reclamation programs and coalfield communities
industries.note: The 20 percent fee cut and the repeal of rural land reclamation grants and Interior Department research contracts would reduce the money available to clean up abandoned mines and acid drainage that pollute water in coal mining regions.

industries.industry: North Slope Borough and Alaska Native communities and corporations
industries.note: The bill would send 50 percent of leasing revenue to Alaska, create an $11 million impact-aid fund for local governments, convey land titles to the Kaktovik Inupiat Corporation and Arctic Slope Regional Corporation, and require best-efforts hiring of Alaska Natives—but local communities would also face industrial development near subsistence hunting grounds.
